strengths: Well-motivated hybrid architecture addressing the trade-off between broad reasoning (frozen LLM) and learning capacity (trainable model)
Systematic exploration of training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO) with concrete evidence for why each fails, showing principled methodology selection
Practical technical contribution: similarity-based data synthesis pipeline with three-phase design that reduces distributional shift and improves training stability
Comprehensive evaluation metrics beyond final performance (hypervolume, uniqueness, diversity, validity) providing nuanced insights
Clear presentation with good motivation, informative figures (especially Figure 1 and co-evolutionary curves), and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: single domain (drug design) with no evaluation on other discrete optimization problems, undermining claims of broad applicability

Critical missing baselines: ExLLM (Ran et al., 2025) and MoLLEO (Wang et al., 2024) are cited as recent benchmarks on the exact same task but are not compared against, preventing validation of state-of-the-art claims
Computational cost and efficiency completely unaddressed: no discussion of API call budgets, wall-clock time comparisons, or training costs despite heavy reliance on proprietary models
Insufficient statistical rigor: no significance tests despite reported standard deviations; some improvements appear modest relative to variance (e.g., HV improvement within noise margins)
Weak ablation studies: many hyperparameters in similarity-based synthesis (α, I₁, I₂, I₃, L, r) without sensitivity analysis; hyperparameter selection process not described
Overclaiming: terms like 'mutual inspiration' and 'co-evolution' are misleading since the frozen API model cannot learn or improve; claims of broad applicability lack supporting evidence
Lack of theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why DPO is ideal, convergence properties, or characterization of when/why the method outperforms alternatives

Limited analysis of method behavior: does not identify problem properties where co-evolution excels, lacks failure case discussion, unclear if distribution shift in local model indicates learning or overfitting

strengths: Clear problem motivation highlighting real limitations of single LLMs and RAG for iterative optimization
Principled empirical investigation of training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO), with honest discussion of failure modes and recovery mechanisms
Thoughtfully designed similarity-based data synthesis to address distributional mismatch between frozen and trainable models
Technically sound implementation with careful attention to training stability and detailed algorithmic specifications
Challenging benchmark extending prior 3-objective drug design to 5 objectives
Comprehensive reproducibility documentation including full algorithms, training details, and ethics statements
weaknesses: Single domain evaluation on drug design only; claims of 'broad applicability' are unsupported and applicability to other discrete optimization domains is unclear
No comparison with key recent baseline ExLLM (Ran et al., 2025) cited as achieving 'strong results'; only compared against own variants and weak single-model baselines

Improvements are modest (0.847±0.138 vs 0.861±0.135 for API-only variants) and often within error margins; large standard deviations (~15-20% of mean) with no statistical significance testing across only 10 runs

Unclear novelty and attribution: DPO training accounts for ~19.5% gain (0.661→0.847), but collaborative component alone adds only ~5% (0.661→0.695); core novelty (similarity-based DPO synthesis) is relatively straightforward
Misleading framing of 'co-evolution': frozen model never learns, only local model trains—relationship is asymmetric one-way adaptation, not mutual inspiration; should be clarified upfront
No ablation studies on critical hyperparameters: α=0.3, similarity windows (I₁, I₂, I₃), global filter [μ±σ], update frequency f; sensitivity analysis completely absent

Key methodological details missing or underspecified: multi-objective scalarization method never specified; training frequency f mentioned as important but values not reported; dataset size L and r parameters vague
Reproducibility hindered by reliance on proprietary paid APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini); hyperparameters incompletely reported (β in DPO, learning rate, epochs); detailed prompt could bias results

Superficial analysis of learned behavior: distribution plot (Fig 3) shows single 1000-molecule sample; no evidence model learns generalizable strategies vs memorizing structures; no analysis of diversity or generalization to unseen prompts

Missing critical comparisons and ablations: no ablation on similarity-based synthesis vs naive DPO; no evaluation on other domains despite 'broad applicability' claims; no computational cost analysis despite expensive API-based approach

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing a genuine problem: combining the exploration capacity of frozen LLMs with the adaptability of trainable models through a principled co-evolutionary approach
Novel similarity-based data synthesis for DPO training (Section 4.3) that effectively mitigates distribution shift between heterogeneous models with clear theoretical justification
Systematic empirical analysis of training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO) with clear explanations for why each succeeds or fails in Section 4.2, providing valuable methodological insights
Convincing experimental results on multi-objective drug design with state-of-the-art Hypervolume Indicator and consistent improvements across multiple metrics (Figure 2, Table 1)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1 framework diagram, Figure 3 co-evolutionary dynamics) and well-structured methodology sections
Thorough algorithmic documentation with detailed implementations in appendix, DPO loss analysis, and training details supporting reproducibility
Complementary analysis techniques including co-evolutionary curves, output distribution shifts, and ablations comparing different model configurations
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope restricted to single domain (drug design); claims of broad applicability to discrete optimization are not empirically validated on other problems (materials design, circuit design, etc.)

Missing direct comparisons with most relevant prior work: ExLLM and MoLLEO are cited but not included in experimental comparisons, making it unclear if improvements derive from the proposed method or simply using two models
Insufficient ablation studies on introduced hyperparameters (α=0.3, similarity intervals I₁/I₂/I₃, μ±σ filter bounds) with no sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness to these choices
Lack of statistical significance testing despite modest improvements in some metrics; 10 runs with mean±std reported but no formal hypothesis tests or confidence intervals
Computational cost and practical deployment considerations not addressed: no analysis of API costs, inference time, or resource requirements compared to baselines
Limited analysis of what the trainable local model actually learns; only one snapshot in Figure 3(right) showing distribution shift without detailed learning curves or pattern analysis
Real-world validation absent: drug design improvements are purely computational with no validation that optimized molecules are actually synthesizable or efficacious in practice

Critical dependency on closed-source APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini) for reproducibility; hardware specifications for local model training not provided; 'anonymous repository' commitment lacks long-term guarantees
Algorithm 1 presented in simplified form in main text requiring readers to consult appendix for actual implementation, reducing transparency of the core contribution
Hyperparameter justification incomplete: why Tanimoto similarity on Morgan fingerprints for molecules? Why μ±σ as the filter? Why these specific interval boundaries? No principled derivation provided

strengths: Well-motivated hybrid architecture addressing genuine limitations of frozen-only and trainable-only LLMs
Systematic and valuable empirical analysis of training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO), documenting failure modes and tradeoffs
Novel similarity-based data synthesis method for constructing stable DPO training pairs, with clear motivation and demonstrated benefits (Figure 6)
Comprehensive experimental design with multiple strong baselines, extensive ablations, orthogonal validation via AutoDock Vina, and demonstration on multiple problem classes
Practical evaluation confirming synthetic accessibility of generated molecules (mean SA=2.00), demonstrating realistic applicability
Detailed appendix, algorithms, and pseudocode supporting reproducibility and transparency
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and thorough documentation of methodology
weaknesses: Empirical improvements marginal and inconsistently supported by statistics: Top-1 improvements overlap within error bars; HV metric shows MCCE (0.847±0.138) lower than GFlowNet mean (0.871±0.288); no statistical significance testing; claims of 'state-of-the-art' overstated

Incomplete cost analysis: Table 8 reports only $3.81 API cost while omitting 8×A800 GPU infrastructure cost (3.12 hours); total computational cost substantially higher than suggested; no fair comparison with baseline methods

Docking validation contradicts narrative: DRD2 and GSK3β show worse binding under orthogonal validation (less negative scores); only JNK3 clearly improves; undermines confidence in optimized molecules' practical value

Limited and unconvincing generalization claims: Circle Packing tested on only 2 instances; MOTSP/MOCVRP results not clearly better than baselines (Table 5); these supplementary experiments insufficient to support general-purpose claims

Strong dependence on domain-specific similarity metrics: embedding-based similarity (4.29) underperforms fingerprint-based (4.35); framework's applicability to new domains where good similarity metrics don't exist is questionable

Fairness concerns in experimental design: expensive API-based GPT-4o not directly comparable to baseline methods; baselines like REINVENT (2017) and GB-GA (2019) dated for 2026; different computational budgets not accounted for

DPO training stability analysis lacks rigor: Figure 4 shows noisy loss with frequent sharp peaks; explanation of peaks as 'new data' is hand-wavy; choice of initial untrained model as reference unconventional and unjustified
Validity metric concerning: MCCE (0.820) substantially lower than GFlowNet (0.998) and DyMol (1.000), indicating more invalid molecules generated—practical liability for drug discovery

Presentation issues: placeholder 'Table ??' on page 6 indicates incomplete revision; diversity metric surprisingly low (0.484) compared to MoLLEO (0.670), contradicting co-evolutionary claims without explanation
Missing methodological details: initialization strategy for local model unclear; no sensitivity analysis for alternation strategy between models; prompt optimization process not justified

strengths: Clear motivation for combining frozen closed-source LLMs with trainable models to enable continuous experience accumulation
Practical similarity-based data synthesis method that effectively stabilizes DPO training in co-evolutionary settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple ablation studies examining design choices
Well-executed presentation with clear figures and detailed appendices providing algorithmic details and supplementary analyses
Extension to multiple combinatorial optimization domains (Circle Packing, MOTSP, MOCVRP) demonstrates potential generalizability
Thorough cost analysis and synthetic accessibility validation demonstrating practical applicability of generated molecules
weaknesses: Confounded experimental design: MCCE combines GPT-4o (exceptionally strong, 2024) + trainable model + DPO, making it unclear whether improvements come from the collaborative framework or simply using a stronger API model; ablation with Gemini shows substantial performance drop

Contradictory SOTA claims: Results are mixed—GFlowNet achieves better Hypervolume (0.871 vs 0.847); Top1 F improvements (4.35 vs 4.23-4.24) are within ±1 standard deviation with no statistical significance testing provided

Limited novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (LLM-based molecular design, DPO fine-tuning, similarity filtering, evolutionary algorithms); the claimed 'co-evolution paradigm' reflects standard evolutionary algorithm design, not novel conceptualization

Insufficient theoretical justification for core design choices: Similarity-based data synthesis lacks formal analysis; why enforcing similarity is optimal unclear; hyperparameter choices (α=0.3, similarity windows) appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

Reproducibility severely limited: Depends critically on proprietary GPT-4o API that may change; code link incomplete in manuscript; extensive hyperparameter tuning space with limited guidance; local compute costs underreported (only API costs shown)

Missing critical ablations and comparisons: No experiment removing the API model entirely to isolate local model contribution; unclear how much improvement stems from collaboration versus simply adding trainable parameters

Overclaimed contributions: Language such as 'paradigm shift,' 'mutual inspiration,' and 'state-of-the-art' overstates incremental engineering work; orthogonal validation (AutoDock Vina) shows mixed and sometimes contradictory results for different objectives

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing the real tension between frozen powerful models and trainable but limited models through collaborative co-evolution
Principled comparison of training paradigms (SFT, RL, DPO) with clear empirical justification for DPO selection
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, orthogonal validation with docking scores, and cost analysis demonstrating practical efficiency
Thorough documentation for reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, implementation details in appendices, and promised code release
Thoughtful similarity-based data synthesis approach that addresses real training instability from contradictory prompt-response pairs
Clear presentation with effective figures and generally well-organized exposition of complex methodology
weaknesses: Primary empirical claim of state-of-the-art performance is not convincingly supported: MCCE (HV=0.847±0.138) does not clearly exceed GFlowNet (0.871±0.288) or DyMol (0.868±0.146); confidence intervals overlap and baselines have numerically higher scores
Critical missing comparison with ExLLM, the most directly relevant baseline that the paper explicitly positions itself against, undermining the motivation for the proposed approach
Limited generalization evidence beyond molecular design: combinatorial experiments show marginal or inconsistent improvements (Circle Packing: +0.0004, MOTSP: underperforms AlphaEvolve)

Method complexity not justified by empirical gains: many hyperparameters (α, similarity intervals I₁/I₂/I₃, update frequency) introduce tuning burden for marginal or statistically unclear improvements

DPO training shows significant loss oscillations (Figure 4) even with similarity filtering; post-hoc explanation lacks rigorous justification and no ablation demonstrates these oscillations don't harm performance
Weak statistical rigor: only 5 runs reported, overlapping confidence intervals prevent clear superiority claims, no significance testing (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon) provided
Presentation errors undermine polish: table reference errors (Table ??) suggest incomplete finalization; overclaiming in abstract/introduction mismatches nuanced results

Limited theoretical justification for design choices: why alternating co-evolution pattern is optimal, no convergence analysis, similarity filtering is empirically motivated without principled guidance
Similarity metric generalization concerns: domain-specific fingerprints for molecules but ad-hoc embedding-based similarity for other domains without principled guidance for new applications
Cost analysis incomplete: hardware amortization not included, no comparison with pure API baseline, results tied to specific GPU configuration (8×A800)
